summary: Defines Proxy Mobile IPv6, a network-based mobility protocol. The network tracks the host's movement and does the signaling for it, so the host needs no mobility software. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Usually your phone has to say where it moved. Here the network does the talking for it, so your phone keeps its address without extra work.

what is a mobile access gateway

subtitle: Mobility for IPv6 hosts without the host doing any mobility signaling: the network does it on the host's behalf.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 needs mobility software in every host's IP stack, which sends signaling messages to its home agent whenever it moves.
tldr.mechanism: A Mobile Access Gateway on the access link detects the host, sends Proxy Binding Updates to a Local Mobility Anchor, and the two set up a bi-directional tunnel. The gateway advertises the host's home network prefix so the host never sees its layer-3 attachment change.
tldr.outcome: A host keeps its address while moving anywhere in the Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain without taking part in signaling. This RFC covers IPv6 only, and it has since been updated by RFC 6543 and RFC 7864.

today: RFC 5213 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6543 and RFC 7864, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself covers only IPv6 prefix mobility over an IPv6 transport network and leaves IPv4 support to a companion document.

sections.title: Network-Based Mobility
sections.content:
IP mobility for IPv6 hosts is defined in Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775). It requires client functionality in the host's IPv6 stack: the mobile node exchanges signaling with a home agent in the network to keep a binding between its home address and its care-of address.

RFC 5213 takes another approach, network-based mobility. A proxy mobility agent in the network performs the signaling with the home agent and manages mobility on behalf of the host. Because it extends Mobile IPv6 signaling and home agent functionality, the protocol is called Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6). The RFC lists two advantages: reuse of the mature home agent functionality and message formats, and a common home agent that serves all types of IPv6 nodes.

The problem statement is documented in RFC 4830.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a phone has to run special software to tell its home base where it went. This design puts that job on the network, so any phone works, even one with no special software.

sections.title: The Players and Their Terms
sections.content:
The Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain is the network where mobility is handled by this protocol. It contains local mobility anchors and mobile access gateways, between which security associations can be set up.

  • Local Mobility Anchor (LMA): the home agent for the mobile node in the domain. It is the topological anchor point for the node's home network prefix(es) and manages its binding state.
  • Mobile Access Gateway (MAG): a function on an access router that tracks the node's movements to and from the access link and signals the node's LMA.
  • Mobile Node (MN): an IP host or router whose mobility is managed by the network. It does not take part in any mobility signaling.
  • Home Network Prefix (MN-HNP): the prefix assigned to the link between the node and the MAG. The node configures its addresses from it.
  • Proxy-CoA: the global address on the MAG's egress interface, which is one end of the tunnel. The LMA records it as the node's care-of address.
  • LMAA: the LMA address that is the other end of the tunnel and the address to which the MAG sends Proxy Binding Updates.

This specification supports the Per-MN-Prefix model, where each node has its own prefix or prefixes, and does not support the Shared-Prefix model. All prefixes assigned to one interface of a node belong to exactly one mobility session.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMA is like a post office that always knows where you live. The MAG is the local mailman at wherever you are now. The mailman keeps telling the post office your latest spot.

sections.title: Attachment and Handoff
sections.content:
When a mobile node attaches to an access link, the MAG identifies it, acquires its identity and checks whether it is authorized for network-based mobility. If so, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the node's LMA. The LMA accepts it, allocates the home network prefix(es), creates a Binding Cache entry and replies with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) that carries the prefix(es).

The MAG then sets up its end of a bi-directional tunnel to the LMA and sends Router Advertisements to the node that advertise the home network prefix(es) as on-link. The node configures its interface using stateful or stateless address configuration, whichever the link permits. From the node's view, the whole domain looks like a single link.

On a handoff, the previous MAG detects the detachment and sends a PBU with a lifetime of 0 to de-register. The LMA accepts but waits before deleting the binding. If the new MAG sends a PBU in that time, the binding is updated, and the node keeps its address configuration. If no PBU arrives, the LMA deletes the Binding Cache entry. The RFC notes the registration from the new MAG may arrive before the de-registration from the old one.

The LMA treats a PBU for an existing session by lifetime and care-of address: a lifetime of 0 means de-registration, a PBU whose Proxy-CoA matches the entry is a lifetime extension without handoff, and any other case is a lifetime extension after handoff.
sections.plainLanguage: When you walk into a new room, the helper there phones head office to say you arrived, and the helper in the old room says you left. Head office waits a short while before forgetting you, in case the new helper is slow.

sections.title: Keeping Updates in Order
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 uses a Sequence Number so the home agent can process binding updates in the order the node sent them. In Proxy Mobile IPv6 the node moves between gateways, and without something like context transfer the new MAG cannot know the last sequence number used. An old PBU delivered late could then point the node's traffic back at the previous MAG.

The RFC adopts two alternatives. The timestamp-based approach has the sender insert the current time of day and the receiver check that it is greater than all previously accepted timestamps. All entities that use it MUST have adequately synchronized clocks, and SHOULD synchronize to a common time source; the Network Time Protocol MAY be used. If clock skew between neighboring MAGs is more than half the reconnection time, the approach SHOULD NOT be used. If the Timestamp option is present, the LMA ignores the Sequence Number field but copies it into the PBA.

The sequence-number-based approach follows Mobile IPv6, but the serving MAG MUST be able to obtain the last sequence number sent for that mobility session, for example through context transfer or a policy store. The RFC leaves how that happens out of scope.

When retransmitting a PBU, a MAG must first check that the node is still attached, uses exponential back-off, and uses a new timestamp or a greater sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: If two notes about where you live arrive out of order, head office might believe the old one. So each note gets a time stamp, and head office only trusts a note newer than the last one it believed.

sections.title: Tunnels and Forwarding
sections.content:
Traffic to the node reaches the LMA, which holds the home network prefix. The LMA forwards it through the bi-directional tunnel to the MAG, which removes the outer header and delivers the packet on the access link. In the other direction, the MAG acts as the node's default router and tunnels the node's packets to the LMA, which removes the outer header and routes the packet on. Packets sent with a link-local source address MUST NOT be forwarded.

This specification supports IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation (RFC 2473) over an IPv6 transport network. IPv4 transport and the other encapsulation modes it lists are left to a companion document. The tunnel header uses the Proxy-CoA as source and the LMAA as destination.

If a correspondent node is attached to the same MAG, the MAG MAY route packets locally instead of tunneling them. The EnableMAGLocalRouting flag controls this, and the RFC warns that the LMA then cannot apply traffic policies or accounting to those flows.

To avoid the node seeing a new default router after every handoff, all MAGs in the domain are required to use the same link-local and link-layer address on any access link. The RFC also warns that this has implications for SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). The MAG SHOULD add an MTU option to its Router Advertisements reflecting the tunnel MTU. For DHCP-based addressing, the MAG acts as a DHCP relay agent and the node must always be assigned an identical set of addresses regardless of link.
sections.plainLanguage: All your mail goes to head office first, which sends it through a private pipe to the local mailman. Your replies go back through the same pipe. If the person you are writing to is in the same building, the mailman may just walk the note over.

sections.title: Messages and Options
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 reuses the Mobile IPv6 Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgement messages, adding a Proxy Registration flag (P). It is 1 for proxy registrations and 0 for direct registrations sent by a mobile node. The LMA MUST ignore and skip mobility options it does not understand.

Both messages can carry these options, at most one of each: Mobile Node Identifier, Home Network Prefix (one or more allowed), Handoff Indicator, Access Technology Type, Timestamp, Mobile Node Link-layer Identifier and Link-local Address.

  • Home Network Prefix: Type 22, Length MUST be 18, with a 16-byte prefix and a prefix length.
  • Handoff Indicator: Type 23, Length MUST be 2, with an 8-bit HI value.
  • Access Technology Type: Type 24, Length MUST be 2, with an 8-bit ATT value.
  • Timestamp: Type 27, Length MUST be 8. The 64-bit value counts seconds since January 1, 1970 in fixed point, with 48 bits for whole seconds and 16 bits for 1/65536 fractions of a second.

The Status field of a PBA is 8 bits. Values below 128 mean the PBU was accepted and higher values mean it was rejected. New values run from 152 to 162, and some values from RFC 3775 are reused.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes between the mailman and head office use a fixed form with small labelled boxes: who you are, which address you were given, how you arrived, and what time it is.

sections.title: Configuration Variables
sections.content:
Section 9 lists variables that system management MUST be able to configure, and their values MUST survive reboots and service restarts.

On the LMA: MinDelayBeforeBCEDelete is how long the LMA waits before deleting a binding after a PBU with lifetime 0 (default 10000 milliseconds). MaxDelayBeforeNewBCEAssign is how long it waits for a de-registration before creating a new session (default 1500 milliseconds). TimestampValidityWindow is the largest allowed difference between a PBU's timestamp and the LMA's clock (default 300 milliseconds).

On the MAG: EnableMAGLocalRouting defaults to 0, meaning all traffic is reverse tunneled to the LMA.

Across the whole domain, and fixed to the same value on every entity: TimestampBasedApproachInUse (default 1), MobileNodeGeneratedTimestampInUse (default 0), and the fixed MAG link-local and link-layer addresses, which an ALL_ZERO value leaves disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the knobs the network owner can turn, like how long head office waits before forgetting you. Each knob comes with a sensible starting setting.

sections.title: Protecting the Signaling
sections.content:
PBU and PBA messages between the MAG and the LMA MUST be protected with security associations that give integrity and data origin authentication. IPsec is mandatory to implement. ESP in transport mode with integrity protection SHOULD be used, confidentiality is not required, and IKEv2 SHOULD be used to set up the associations. Protecting the node's data traffic with ESP in tunnel mode is optional.

Because the node takes no part in signaling, the LMA MUST restrict the creation and manipulation of proxy bindings to specifically authorized MAGs and prefixes, using local configuration. Without this, a malicious node could hijack a mobility session or mount a denial of service.

The RFC also requires trust between the MAG and the node, with the node authenticated and authorized before it gets network access, and it suggests the LMA may check with a trusted entity that the node really is attached to the MAG, to address a compromised MAG.
sections.plainLanguage: Head office only listens to helpers on its approved list, and the notes are sealed so nobody can fake or change them on the way.
